A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MARASON study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original MARASON experiments on NIST, including spectral similarity, molecular retrieval, component ablations, and fragment-matching analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds MARASON results on MassSpecGym, a reference-similarity analysis, and a spectrum-level case study.

M1.justification: The main architecture and Eqs. (1)–(7) remain unchanged. v2 adds a collision-energy pseudo-labeling adaptation for MassSpecGym training and proposes switching to non-RAG prediction when reference Tanimoto similarity is at most 0.2; evaluation of that combined switching rule is not reported. The expanded Fig. 2 caption supplies architectural detail rather than establishing a redesigned matcher.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates NIST data, including random/scaffold splits and the protonated-adduct subset. v2 retains this coverage and adds training and evaluation on MassSpecGym, extending evidence to another molecular dataset with fewer annotated spectra and incomplete collision-energy labels. The CANOPUS-to-NPLIB1 wording change concerns an excluded dataset, not changed experimental coverage.

E2.justification: The Random comparator is removed from Table 1, while the learned NIST baselines and matching-method ablations remain. NEIMS (FFN), NEIMS (GNN), and FraGNNet in the new MassSpecGym comparison were already evaluated in v1's main text or appendix; they are not newly introduced baseline families.

E3.justification: v2 adds a distinct MassSpecGym protocol: generating missing collision-energy labels with a NIST-pretrained model, training MARASON from scratch, and reporting formula-known retrieval at top-1, top-5, and top-20. It also introduces evaluation stratified by reference Tanimoto similarity with a non-RAG control. The existing NIST splits, spectral binning, and retrieval procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and fragment-matching examples, v2 directly tests dependence on reference quality through RAG versus non-RAG comparisons across Tanimoto bins (Table 4, Sec. 4.2.6). It also adds a full-spectrum prediction case study (Fig. 4). These extend analysis to an important applicability boundary; the similarity analysis uses existing reference pairs, with no samples in the lowest bin.

E5.justification: The new MassSpecGym table reports 99.9% bootstrap confidence intervals using 20,000 resamples, with MARASON's training seed fixed at 1. Table 1 changes its uncertainty description from 1.96 standard deviations to 95% confidence intervals while retaining identical errors and three seeds. No recalculation is established, and appendix captions retain the standard-deviation description.

E6.justification: Retained NIST scores are unchanged, including MARASON's 0.278 top-1 accuracy. New MassSpecGym results report 0.3403 top-1 accuracy versus FraGNNet's 0.3193 (Table 2). Table 4 adds reference-quality results, including 0.550 versus 0.566 without RAG in the (0.1, 0.2] bin. Fig. 4 adds a spectrum example scoring 0.935 versus 0.797 without RAG. Table 1's Random results are removed.

T1.justification: The assignment formulations, graph-embedding equations, matching definitions, and intensity-prediction expression in Eqs. (1)–(7) are unchanged. Neither version supplies additional theoretical propositions or proofs, and the appendices remain empirical.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims about neural graph matching for molecular RAG and MARASON's approximately 28% versus 19% retrieval accuracy. MassSpecGym supplies additional supporting evidence without redefining those core contributions.

C2.justification: Sec. 4.2.6 adds a practical qualification: retrieval offers little benefit with very dissimilar references and can slightly hurt, motivating a suggested non-RAG fallback. The new spectrum example explains alignment despite shifted peak masses. An Impact Statement adds discussion of demographic bias in reference databases; existing mechanism explanations and appendix failure interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of future code release with a public repository link, expands Fig. 2's explanation of separate GNN weights, and documents the MassSpecGym pseudo-labeling and retraining steps. However, it removes the Software and Data section containing NIST purchasing information and the licensed-user pretrained-weight access statement. Hardware and existing implementation settings are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the MassSpecGym benchmark reference by Bushuiev et al. (2024) and removes Li, P. et al. (2024) alongside the introductory protein-structure example. The substantive positioning around molecular RAG, neural graph matching, and ICEBERG remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 refines terminology from MS to MS/MS, shortens an introductory example, expands the architecture caption, and adds two results subsections and an Impact Statement while removing Software and Data. Most existing prose, the main section sequence, and appendix organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a four-panel spectrum comparison and tables for MassSpecGym and reference-similarity bins, expands Fig. 2's caption, and removes the Random row from Table 1. Existing displays retain their designs and mostly undergo relocation or renumbering; the appendix fragment-pair graphics are unchanged.

improvement.justification: MassSpecGym evaluation broadens empirical support beyond NIST, and Table 4 provides useful evidence about when retrieval helps or hurts. The spectrum example and stated code availability also improve assessability and reuse. These gains are tempered by limited pseudo-labeling detail, unexplained relabeling of unchanged Table 1 error bars as confidence intervals, and removal of data/weight access information. Overall, v2 strengthens validation and practical interpretation without substantially revising the underlying study.
